subsystems.name: The superconductor itself
subsystems.role: a crystal lattice in which electrons pair up and flow with zero resistance at ordinary temperature and pressure.
parts: hydrogen-rich hydride, cuprate or nickelate lattice
dopant or strain layer that tunes the electron count
capping layer to keep the phase stable in air

subsystems.name: Synthesis route
subsystems.role: makes the phase in the first place, usually by squeezing it into existence.
parts: diamond anvil or large-volume high-pressure cell

subsystems.name: Verification and metrology
subsystems.role: proves the effect is real rather than a measurement artefact.

subsystems.name: Conductor fabrication
subsystems.role: turns a brittle ceramic-like material into a flexible current-carrying wire.

subsystems.name: Coil and magnet engineering
subsystems.role: winds the conductor into useful field shapes and survives faults.

subsystems.name: System integration
subsystems.role: connects the conductor to grids, motors or fusion magnets.
parts: current leads and cryogenic or conductive cooling
circuit breakers and fault current limiters

buildSteps.title: Predict a candidate composition
buildSteps.detail: Computational screening (density-functional theory plus machine learning) searches for lattices with strong electron pairing or the right electronic structure.

buildSteps.title: Synthesise it under pressure
buildSteps.detail: A few micrograms of precursor are loaded into a diamond anvil cell and squeezed to 100–200 gigapascals — pressures found deep inside the Earth — while a laser heats the sample to form the desired phase.

buildSteps.title: Prove the effect is genuine
buildSteps.detail: Resistance is measured with four contacts while temperature and magnetic field are swept. A true superconductor shows a sharp drop to zero, expels magnetic field (the Meissner effect) and shows a matching jump in specific heat. Each check guards against a different artefact: shorted current paths, a metal-to-insulator transition, or a pressure-driven structural change.

buildSteps.title: Stabilise the phase at ambient pressure
buildSteps.detail: This is the unsolved step. Chemical pressure (substituting larger or smaller atoms), epitaxial strain in thin films, nanoscale layering, or rapid quenching from high pressure might let the structure survive when the anvil is released.

buildSteps.title: Scale the synthesis
buildSteps.detail: Moving from micrograms inside an anvil to grams and kilograms requires high-pressure furnaces, vapour or solution deposition, or roll-to-roll film growth — whichever route can be run continuously and cheaply.

buildSteps.title: Draw it into wire
buildSteps.detail: Brittle superconducting material cannot simply be drawn like copper. It is either packed as powder inside a metal tube and rolled, or grown as a thin film on a flexible buffered metal tape, then clad with silver and copper to carry current if the superconductor briefly warms.

buildSteps.title: Wind and protect coils
buildSteps.detail: The tape is wound into coils for magnets, motors or cables. Because a coil stores megajoules of energy, quench detection and protection must dump that energy safely if any section warms above its critical temperature.

buildSteps.title: Qualify in a system
buildSteps.detail: The conductor is tested inside a real magnet, cable, generator or maglev bogie and cycled thermally and electrically for years to prove it does not degrade.

prerequisites.why: diamond anvil cells and large-volume presses can already reach the pressures where superconductivity appears near room temperature.
supercomputers can screen candidate lattices far faster than trial-and-error experiments.
flexible high-temperature superconducting tape is made in kilometre lengths, but only works while cooled with liquid nitrogen.
every verified near-room-temperature superconductor so far collapses back to a non-superconducting structure once the pressure is removed.
several dramatic claims of room-temperature superconductivity have been retracted, so the field needs agreed, independent testing protocols.

pathway.milestone: hydride superconductors confirmed near 250 K (about −23 °C) but only at roughly 170 gigapascals
pathway.unlocks: proof that chemistry can push critical temperatures close to ambient — while showing how far pressure must still fall.

pathway.milestone: similar temperatures at tens of gigapascals instead of hundreds, using chemical substitution or strain
pathway.unlocks: larger samples and easier measurement, plus a credible route to releasing the pressure entirely.

pathway.milestone: a phase that superconducts above 0 °C at ordinary pressure, independently replicated by several labs
pathway.unlocks: the scientific milestone; attention shifts to manufacturing.

pathway.milestone: conductor made in kilometre lengths at a cost comparable to copper
pathway.unlocks: lossless transmission cables, lighter and more efficient motors and generators, and cheaper MRI without liquid helium.

pathway.milestone: deployment in grids, maglev lines and compact fusion magnets
pathway.unlocks: large cuts in transmission losses and a shrinking of the cooling plant that today dominates superconducting systems.
